set.st: Old Niles people said the French fort just above the dam (Fort St. Joseph) was massacred by Indians, and that gold was thrown into the fort's well and more buried on the river bank. The fort stood 'up the river from Niles, near a mile'; its well was 'near two crab apple trees' older residents remembered, and 'a large amount of French sovereigns' were thrown in, but floods soon filled it and it was never found. The last to hunt for it was the late Robert Chambers, 'who tilled the premises'. Prof. E. E. Crane collected silver buttons, bracelets and crucifixes on the site and sold them to the Northern Indiana Historical Society. The late Ransom Dopp (a stage driver in 1848, later owner of about 1,500 acres in Wayne Twp, Cass Co) was rumoured to have found the bank cache: he was seen digging on the river bank, stopped suddenly, and then bought a large tract. The Dowagiac Republican, answering, said his neighbours doubted it. The Niles editor had heard the tale more than 50 years earlier from the Indian Bertrand. In Dec 1898, answering the Chicago Chronicle's Bertrand story, the Niles Daily Star had already noted that locals told of a large sum buried 'just above the dam in this city' in the French and Indian war.
pinev: 1889 Sanborn, Niles, sheet 6: DAM across the St Joseph between the Michigan Wood Pulp Co. and the Ohio Paper Co. mills, '3/4 mile S. of Main St'.

2015 1 m LiDAR: the flattened river surface steps up about 4.2 m (194.7 m to 198.9 m) at about 41.8175, -86.2588, which is the dam; pin about 150 m upstream of it. Moved from a pin about 2 km north, off the river.
The 1899 account places the fort 'just above the dam', matching the Fort St. Joseph site on the E bank upstream of the dam; pin unchanged.
'Near a mile' up river from Niles (May 1899) = the Fort St. Joseph site; pin unchanged.
